passage: Omar had prayed every night for a week that the school trip to the lake would be sunny. On Saturday morning rain drummed on his window in Rotterdam. He pulled the blanket over his head, then dragged himself to the kitchen and pushed his cereal around the bowl. What if nobody is listening? Grandpa Ivan put down his cup. "You're quiet." "I prayed and it still rained," Omar said. "Maybe it doesn't work." Grandpa Ivan did not scold him. "That's an honest thing to wonder. I've wondered it myself. Shall we walk to the bakery and talk?"

qa.q: What did Omar pray for every night for a week?
qa.a: He prayed that the school trip to the lake would be sunny.

qa.q: What might Omar be worried about as he pushes his cereal around the bowl?
qa.a: He is wondering whether anyone is really listening to his prayers, since he prayed hard and it still rained.

qa.q: What could Omar do with his doubt?
qa.a: Keep talking with Grandpa Ivan, who offered a walk, rather than hiding the doubt or feeling wicked for having it.

qa.q: How does Grandpa Ivan see Omar's question?
qa.a: As an honest thing to wonder; he says he has wondered it himself, so he does not treat it as wrong.

grounding: Illustrates a child whose prayed-for wish fails, doubts whether anyone hears, and is met by a welcoming elder.

passage: The bell for the Diwali break hadn't even rung when Vidya bounced on her chair. "Twelve guests on Saturday, a new orange lehenga, and Mummy is making besan laddoos!" Raghav grinned. "I'm getting sparklers." Their teacher set a box on the front table. It was for sweets and diyas for the cleaners' families, who work through the holidays. Vidya went quiet. She thought of the cleaner who always said "good morning, beta." At the end of class she stopped by the table. "Ma'am, can I bring some laddoos tomorrow?" "The box stays here till the last day," the teacher said.

qa.q: How many guests is Vidya expecting on Saturday?
qa.a: She is expecting twelve guests.

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling as she talked about Diwali, and what changed when the box appeared?
qa.a: She was bubbling with excitement; when the teacher explained the box for the cleaners' families, she went quiet, thought of the cleaner who greets her, and wanted to share.

qa.q: How might Vidya share without losing her own joy?
qa.a: Bring a small box of laddoos to add to the box, as she asked, while still enjoying her own celebration.

qa.q: How might the cleaners' families feel to receive sweets and diyas?
qa.a: Remembered and included in the festival, even though they work through the holidays.

grounding: Illustrates a child bubbling with festival excitement who remembers those who cannot celebrate and shares a little.

passage: Rain hammered the tarpaulin over the colony's festival ground and everyone squeezed under it to sing. Mohit, eight, ducked in among the other children, dripping. A man holding a steel ladle stepped in front of him. "Not you. Your family isn't one of ours." The singing carried on behind the man's back. Mohit's ears burned and water ran down his neck. He did not understand what he had done. He stood at the edge in the rain until his Masi Sudha arrived with an umbrella and saw his face. He told her in a rush. She put her arm around him. "That was not because of anything you did. Come, I'm going to speak to the organisers."

qa.q: What was the man in front of Mohit holding?
qa.a: He was holding a steel ladle.

qa.q: What was Mohit feeling and thinking as he stood at the edge in the rain?
qa.a: He was hurt and confused: his ears burned and he did not understand what he had done.

qa.q: Who could Mohit tell, and what does that do for him?
qa.a: He can tell a trusted adult like Masi Sudha, who reassures him it was not because of anything he did and goes to speak up for him 🤍.

qa.q: How might Masi Sudha see what happened?
qa.a: As unfair to a child: she put her arm around him and went to speak to the organisers.

grounding: Illustrates a child told he cannot join a community gathering because of who his family is, hurt and confused, and turning to a trusted adult.

passage: Friday. Today Leela didn't eat the gulab jamun at lunch even though she loves it. I asked why, and I tried to ask nicely. She said she gave up sweets until Easter, a thing she does with her family to remember Jesus. Then she showed me the small cross on her chain, from her grandmother. I said Mummy fasts on Mondays and we don't eat dinner before the lamp is lit. Leela said, "That's kind of like mine!" 🙂 I asked if I could ask her more things sometime. She said yes. Different, but both real, I think. - Chetan

qa.q: What did Leela give up until Easter?
qa.a: She gave up sweets until Easter.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling when Chetan asked Leela about the gulab jamun, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Chetan was curious and wanted to be kind: the diary says Chetan tried to ask nicely, and the questions came from wanting to understand, not to judge.

qa.q: How could Chetan keep learning about Leela's faith respectfully?
qa.a: Keep asking kindly, listen to the answers, and check that Leela is happy to explain, as Leela said yes to more questions.

qa.q: How might Leela feel about Chetan's questions?
qa.a: Probably comfortable and glad, since Chetan asked nicely, shared about Chetan's own family, and Leela agreed to more questions.

grounding: Illustrates a child curious about a friend's fasting and cross who asks kindly and listens.

passage: Monday. Gurleen invited Kishore to the gurdwara on Saturday for Baisakhi. Kishore asked Mummy first, and she smiled and told him to go and listen well. Saturday. Gurleen handed him a scarf for his head and whispered what each thing was: why everyone sits on the floor, what the warm sweet prasad is, why they all eat together in the langar. Kishore folded his hands the way Gurleen did and felt welcome. Monday. At school he told a classmate about the prasad. "Did you pray too?" the classmate asked. "I listened," Kishore said. "My own prayers are still mine. But I liked being there."

qa.q: What did Gurleen hand Kishore at the gurdwara?
qa.a: Gurleen handed him a scarf for his head.

qa.q: How did Kishore feel at the gurdwara, and what shows he was not worried about his own faith?
qa.a: He felt welcome; afterwards he said his own prayers were still his, but that he liked being there.

qa.q: How can a child join a friend's festival with respect and still keep their own faith?
qa.a: Listen, follow the customs politely, ask questions, and stay clear that joining does not mean having to agree, as Kishore did.

qa.q: How might Gurleen have felt showing Kishore around?
qa.a: Probably glad and proud to share, since Gurleen whispered patient explanations of each thing 🙂.

grounding: Illustrates a child welcomed to a friend's festival with patient explanations, joining respectfully without feeling threatened.

passage: Note from the Class 5 teacher. At recess three boys imitated Gargi's short prayer before lunch, folding their hands and gabbling. Harsha laughed along with them, loudly at first. Gargi closed the tiffin and walked away, and Harsha's laugh stopped, leaving a stiff smile. When one boy started the act again, Harsha said, "Let's go and play." Afterwards I spoke with Harsha privately. Harsha said, "Everybody was laughing, so I did. I felt bad when Gargi left." I did not scold. We talked about what Harsha could do next time, and I will keep an eye on how the group treats Gargi.

qa.q: How many boys imitated Gargi's prayer?
qa.a: Three boys imitated Gargi's prayer.

qa.q: What was Harsha feeling when Gargi closed the tiffin and walked away?
qa.a: Regret: Harsha's laugh stopped, and later Harsha said they joined in because everybody was laughing and felt bad when Gargi left.

qa.q: What braver choice could Harsha make next time?
qa.a: Stand quietly aside or change the subject, as Harsha began to do by saying, "Let's go and play."

qa.q: How might Gargi have felt during the imitation?
qa.a: Hurt and embarrassed, which is probably why Gargi closed the tiffin and walked away.

grounding: Illustrates a child laughing at a classmate's prayer to fit in, feeling bad, and starting to change the subject.

passage: In the school cloakroom in Gothenburg, two classmates pointed at the round cap Lars wore on Fridays. "Funny hat!" one giggled, and the other copied the way he bowed at prayer time. Lars pulled the cap off and stuffed it in his bag, face burning. He felt there was something wrong with being who he was. At lunch he pushed his fish around the plate. Daniel slid onto the bench beside him. "I like your cap," Daniel said. "Want to tell the teacher?" Lars nodded slowly. That evening he told his mother too. She held his hand and said the cap was nothing to be ashamed of.

qa.q: Where did the classmates point at Lars's cap?
qa.a: They pointed at it in the school cloakroom.

qa.q: What did Lars feel about himself after being mocked?
qa.a: He felt ashamed, as if there were something wrong with being who he was; his face was burning and he hid the cap in his bag.

qa.q: What steps could help Lars now?
qa.a: Tell the teacher, as he agreed to, and lean on Daniel and his mother, who both show that nothing is wrong with his cap.

qa.q: How might Daniel have seen that moment?
qa.a: As unfair to a friend: Daniel sat next to Lars, said he liked the cap, and suggested telling the teacher.

grounding: Illustrates a child mocked for his prayer cap, feeling ashamed, and supported by a friend, a teacher and his mother.

passage: In the clinic waiting room, Nana turned a page of his newspaper and muttered, "Those church people are not good, you know." Uma looked at the poster on the wall, her cheeks hot. Her friend Jaya went to church, and on Tuesday Jaya had shared half a tiffin when Uma forgot hers. Uma did not want to be rude. "Nana," she said, "Jaya shared her lunch with me on Tuesday. She's really kind." Nana gave a small grunt and turned another page without answering. Uma stayed quiet, still confused, but sure of what she had seen herself.

qa.q: Where were Uma and Nana when he made the remark?
qa.a: They were in the clinic waiting room.

qa.q: Why did Uma feel confused when Nana spoke?
qa.a: Nana said church people are not good, but her friend Jaya, who goes to church, had been kind to her.

qa.q: How can Uma keep her own view without being rude to Nana?
qa.a: Speak politely from her own experience, as she did about the shared lunch, and keep asking questions when it feels right.

qa.q: How might Nana see Uma's reply?
qa.a: Nana may feel surprised or a bit uncomfortable; he grunted and turned the page without answering, so what he thinks is not clear.

grounding: Illustrates a child confused by an elder's prejudice against a friend's faith who holds to her own experience politely.

passage: Sit down, beta, I'll tell you about my friend Kamal. I'm Arohi, and I was ten then. During Ramzan, Kamal fasted in the school heat, and at recess an older boy jeered, "What a stupid thing to do. Starving yourself for nothing." Everyone laughed a little. My knees felt like jelly. But I stood up and said, "Don't talk about his fast like that. It's his religion and he's my friend." The whole yard went quiet. The older boy shrugged and walked off. Kamal only nodded at me, but the next day he saved me the seat beside him.

qa.q: How old was Arohi in the story?
qa.a: Arohi was ten.

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling as she stood up to speak?
qa.a: Arohi was frightened and uncomfortable, since Arohi's knees felt like jelly, but Arohi spoke anyway rather than stay silent about a friend.

qa.q: What would you advise a child who hears someone insult a friend's religion?
qa.a: Say calmly that it is not right to talk that way about a friend's faith, and check on the friend afterwards.

qa.q: How might Kamal have seen Arohi speaking up?
qa.a: As real support: Kamal nodded and saved Arohi the seat the next day, and probably felt less alone.

grounding: Illustrates a child speaking up despite discomfort when a friend's religion is insulted.

passage: Republic Day morning on the village school ground was cold and bright. The flag climbed to the top of the pole and snapped open in the wind. When the anthem began, Dhruv stood so tall his neck ached, and goosebumps ran up both arms. Beside him, Manoj leaned on his crutch, standing as straight as he could, his hand trembling with effort. After the last line, sweets were handed out. Dhruv carried a stool across to Manoj. "Sit. The sweets are coming." "I was fine," said Manoj, sitting anyway, grinning.

qa.q: What did Manoj lean on during the anthem?
qa.a: He leaned on his crutch.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling during the anthem?
qa.a: Deep pride: he stood so tall his neck ached and goosebumps ran up both arms.

qa.q: How did Dhruv show love for his country in a caring way?
qa.a: He noticed a classmate's effort and carried a stool over to Manoj after the anthem.

qa.q: How might Manoj have felt about the stool?
qa.a: He said he was fine but sat anyway, grinning, so he probably appreciated the thought while not wanting to be fussed over 😊.

grounding: Illustrates a child's pride during the anthem on Republic Day, joined with care for a classmate.
